summary:
Recommendation: move the wordpress MySQL database to three AWS services in three waves, with the target schemas designed for all three. Wave 1 moves it to Aurora MySQL, which serves 62.6% of the queries. Wave 2 puts ElastiCache in front of 20 hot reads, which carry 83.4% of calls. Wave 3 moves 37.4% of the queries to DynamoDB. The projected cost of the full modernization is $513 per month at AWS Price List on-demand prices for us-east-1, retrieved 2026-10-25. No current cost was collected for the source database, so the plan claims no saving against it.

Risk: overall risk is medium. Two exposures drive it: reads on DynamoDB-side copies kept in sync by change data capture (CDC), and queries where two engines scored almost the same. Set up CDC and confirm the engine for those queries before wave 3 starts.

Decision: approve wave 1. It moves the database 1:1 to Aurora MySQL, the same engine family as MySQL, with its current data model, and its cutover waits until schema and data parity is validated against the source.

Cache layer: ElastiCache fronts 20 designed cached reads (83.4% of calls) cache-aside and owns no queries. Schema design produced 50 target objects: 107 queries in 57 query groups; 120 in-scope access patterns (Aurora MySQL: 20 target tables, 67 in-scope access patterns; DynamoDB: 17 target tables, 35 in-scope access patterns; ElastiCache: 13 key designs, 18 in-scope access patterns). The schema design's table map lists 22 source tables (Aurora MySQL, DynamoDB, ElastiCache). Estimated monthly cost: $512.58. 7 open migration risks (overall: MEDIUM); 5 more were resolved by the assignment. Top query groups by throughput: Option lookups, Post reads, API key access. Other targets evaluated: DocumentDB (consolidated into Aurora MySQL by the reality check), OpenSearch (consolidated into Aurora MySQL by the reality check).

risks.description: [aurora_mysql] The Aurora MySQL schema design records 2 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
details: The heavy order-total aggregations join wp_posts to wp_postmeta by repeated self-joins on meta_key. They are kept on Aurora MySQL and sent to a reader instead of being redesigned

risks.description: [dynamodb] The DynamoDB schema design records 24 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
details: API key authentication (query `1794daed`) reads through the ApiKeysByConsumerKey index, which projects user_id, permissions, consumer_secret and nonces so the read needs no base-table fetch. The last_access update (query `0452bed2`) changes no projected attribute, so it writes only the base item

Auto-increment IDs (`wp_posts.ID`, `wp_actionscheduler_actions.action_id`, the metadata `meta_id` columns) are assigned by the application as time-ordered 64-bit integers, and each insert (queries `445ec39b`, `7ead756f`) is a `PutItem` with `attribute_not_exists` on the key

Comments and their meta rows share one item collection keyed by comment_id: the comment is the item with sort key COMMENT and each meta row is an item with sort key META# followed by the meta_id zero-padded to 20 digits. Query `65f7884e` reads a comment's meta rows in meta_id order from that partition; query `7346ea7e` reads the comment with GetItem

Increment and decrement updates on `meta_value` (queries `2c0093ed`, `33dfdb12`) run as `UpdateItem` with `ADD`, which needs a number. Keys updated this way are stored with the number type in `meta_value`; every other key stays a string

Large text columns stay inline: `post_content`, `post_content_filtered`, `post_excerpt`, `post_title`, `to_ping`, `pinged` and the `meta_value` columns. Average source rows are 711 B for posts, 144 B for post metadata and 131 B for order item metadata, against the 400 KB item limit

Posts and their metadata share one item collection in `wp_posts`: the post is the item with sort key `POST` and each metadata row is an item with sort key `META#<meta_key>`, both under the partition key `post_id`

Query `329367a2` scanned wp_wc_tax_rate_classes. The 2 rows now sit in one partition under the constant key TAX_RATE_CLASS, with a sort key of name followed by the class id, so the read is one Query that returns them ordered by name
Query `3440484f` filters a post by ID and `post_type`. The key `post_id` identifies the item, so the read is a `GetItem` and the application compares `post_type` on the returned item

Query `50b46567` read all metadata of a list of terms with full table scans in the source (7,741 scans). It becomes one Query per `term_id` on the `wp_termmeta` partition key, and the sort key is `meta_key` instead of `meta_id`

Text columns stay inline in the items: comment_content is capped at 65535 bytes in the source and wp_comments averages 552 bytes per row against the 400 KB item limit; meta_value is a longtext whose table is estimated at 52429 bytes per row, also under the limit

The autoload load (query `413c99e4`) reads the `OptionsByAutoload` index, partitioned on `autoload` and projecting `option_value`, so the Query returns about 247 items without a base-table fetch. `autoload` has few distinct values, so one partition value holds the loaded options; its read load of about 500 read units per second and write load of about 129 write units per second at design rates stay under the per-partition limits

The comment count of query `8c66eaee` moves from COUNT(*) over a post's comments to a counter item in PostCommentCounts, keyed by post and approval status. The comment insert (query `de9a7ba3`) writes the comment and adds 1 to the counter in one TransactWriteItems call

The key of each metadata table is (parent id, `meta_key`), so one item holds one value per key. The source allows several rows with the same post_id and meta_key, and the migration finds them before load

The log table wp_actionscheduler_logs is keyed by action_id with log_id as the sort key, and the insert (query `b05af520`) is a PutItem with attribute_not_exists(log_id). The source log_id is an auto-increment, so new entries need an application-generated, increasing id
The meta_value column stays inline on wp_usermeta items: the table averages 16478 bytes per row against the 400 KB item limit, and the design counts it at 1 KB per item (1328 bytes per item)
The order_item_name column (text, 65535 bytes maximum) stays inline on wp_woocommerce_order_items: the table averages 129 bytes per row against the 400 KB item limit

The two key-scoped writes, query `77cd1ad7` on wp_wc_reserved_stock and query `2264704d` on wp_woocommerce_downloadable_product_permissions, use order_id as the partition key of their tables. Each write Queries the order's items by key and then deletes or updates them item by item

The update by name (query `ac34da34`) carries `attribute_exists(option_name)`, matching the source UPDATE, which changes only a row that exists. The upsert (query `a13f5749`) is an unconditional PutItem that replaces the whole item
The usermeta IN-list read (query `3a74580e`) becomes one Query per user_id on wp_usermeta, keyed by user_id with umeta_id as the sort key

`option_value` (longtext) stays inline in the item. The table's average item is 360 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, and the schema-wide item size estimate is 1283 bytes with the text column counted at 1 KB

`wp_options` becomes one DynamoDB table keyed by `option_name`, the column carrying the unique index in the source, so the lookups, upsert, update and delete (queries `66c96f95`, `e223aefb`, `ac34da34`, `a13f5749`, `216d92b3`) are single-item operations by key. The auto-increment `option_id` is kept as a plain attribute
wp_term_relationships is keyed by object_id and term_taxonomy_id, and the source index on term_taxonomy_id alone is not carried over because query `0d20f1d9` reads by the full key

wp_wc_product_meta_lookup becomes the table ProductMetaLookup keyed by product_id, and REPLACE INTO (query `d72966f8`) becomes a PutItem that overwrites the whole item. The secondary indexes of the source table (sku, price range, stock and sale flags) have no read query in this group, so none is created
wp_woocommerce_order_items is keyed by order_item_id alone and carries no index on order_id, which the source table indexes. No query in this part reads order items by order_id
risks.mitigation: Review these trade-offs with the team that builds DynamoDB before Wave 3 starts, and test each one the application depends on.

risks.description: [elasticache] The ElastiCache schema design records 5 trade-offs to review, listed under Migration trade-offs in the engineering report.
details: Post list and title lookups (queries `f31a66f5`, `d4bf16d6` and `52da34b1`) are cached as sorted sets of IDs, one key per distinct status filter
Postmeta and order item meta are stored as one hash per parent with a JSON array of values per meta_key, not one key per row
Posts, post metadata and options are cached with event-driven deletes plus a TTL of 10 to 60 minutes
Scheduler action reads use TTLs of 15 and 30 seconds instead of delete-on-write, because the status of a row changes on every queue run
The term joins of queries `d5ae7abb`, `4481cc0c` and `2389b8a0` are precomputed per object and per term instead of joined at read time
risks.mitigation: Review these trade-offs with the team that builds ElastiCache before Wave 2 starts, and test each one the application depends on.

risks.description: [dynamodb] Routing did not penalise DynamoDB for the frequent-full-scan finding the source shows on 1 query, because the design removes the read it is about (each query's evidence says how).
details: A whole read of a small reference table, which the design keeps as one item collection or caches.
risks.mitigation: Design this query in DynamoDB as each one's evidence says before the Wave 3 gate, and serve none of them as a scan.

mitigation_strategies: Before the Wave 1 gate, close RISK-003 and RISK-004 (logic moved to the application and design trade-offs).
Before the Wave 2 gate, close RISK-006 (design trade-offs).
Before the Wave 3 gate, close RISK-001, RISK-002, RISK-005 and RISK-007 (tables kept in sync, close calls, design trade-offs and redesigns routing relies on).

After wave 1 (Aurora MySQL): compare the latency of 107 queries with their source baseline (weighted average 1.6 ms) and check the engine sustains the design rate of 3,862.4 requests/s before starting wave 2.
After wave 2 (ElastiCache): track the cache hit rate for the 20 hot reads it fronts on Aurora MySQL (83.4% of calls, 185.1 calls/s) and compare their latency with the source before starting wave 3.
After wave 3 (DynamoDB): compare the latency of 40 queries with their source baseline (weighted average 1.98 ms) and check the engine sustains the design rate of 3,765.9 requests/s.

resolved_risks.description: [aurora_mysql] Moved to DynamoDB: Single-row SELECT by primary key at very high frequency (more than 30 calls/second). Aurora serves it natively with a B-tree point read and scales reads with up to 15 Aurora Replicas (Amazon Aurora User Guide, Replication with Amazon Aurora).
resolved_risks.reason: the Aurora MySQL analysis recommended DynamoDB for these queries and the assignment moved them there

resolved_risks.description: [aurora_mysql] Kept on Aurora MySQL because of a utility or DDL statement and multi-table joins on this table.
resolved_risks.reason: Aurora MySQL is also required for a utility or DDL statement and multi-table joins on this table, so keeping it there is a deliberate routing decision, not an open risk; revisit DynamoDB for this table's simple key-value reads in a later wave if those other queries are retired or move too

resolved_risks.description: [aurora_mysql] Moved to DynamoDB: Table with no foreign keys and no join participation: all queries are single-table CRUD. Aurora serves single-table CRUD natively and uses none of its relational features for it (Amazon Aurora User Guide, What is Amazon Aurora).
resolved_risks.reason: the Aurora MySQL analysis recommended DynamoDB for these queries and the assignment moved them there

resolved_risks.description: [aurora_mysql] Moved to DynamoDB: Table accessed by at most 2 distinct query patterns, all single-table, all by primary key or single column filter. Aurora serves these reads natively and its query optimizer adds nothing to them (Amazon Aurora User Guide, What is Amazon Aurora).
resolved_risks.reason: the Aurora MySQL analysis recommended DynamoDB for these queries and the assignment moved them there

resolved_risks.description: [dynamodb] GROUP BY, HAVING, or an aggregate over rows no key anchors or over a join (one key's COUNT or SUM is a Query on that key, not this pattern). DynamoDB has no server-side aggregation: a Query or Scan can only count the items it reads (Select = COUNT), so a grouped result needs the application layer, pre-computed aggregates or a separate analytics store (Amazon DynamoDB API Reference, Query).
resolved_risks.reason: the queries run as SQL on Aurora MySQL

optimizations.recommendation: Reorder the composite index to (post_type, post_status, post_date, ID) so the equality filters on post_type and post_status lead and post_date serves the ORDER BY.
optimizations.rationale: Listing queries such as `12f856ea` filter on post_type and post_status and sort by post_date DESC, examining about 15,790 rows per call. The draft index starts with ID, which no filter uses.

optimizations.recommendation: Add composite indexes on (post_id, meta_key) and (order_item_id, meta_key).
optimizations.rationale: Lookups by owner id and meta_key (queries `3dbc7d9a` at 14.6 calls per second and `22cb9563`) currently examine 10 to 19 rows to return under one. The composite index resolves them in one probe.

optimizations.recommendation: Route the read-only reporting queries (order totals `a0b655ea`, order item counts `fc99562b`) to an Aurora Replica reader endpoint.
optimizations.rationale: These aggregations examine 369,349 and 82,874 rows per call and take 911 ms and 215 ms. Running them on a reader keeps them off the writer that serves page requests.

trade_offs.description: The schema carries over 1:1 from the MySQL source. No column types change, and only three index changes are made: a reordered wp_posts composite index and two composite meta lookup indexes.
trade_offs.impact: Migration risk stays low and WordPress and WooCommerce run unmodified. The three new or reordered indexes add a small amount of storage and write cost, in return for fewer rows examined on the busiest lookups.

trade_offs.description: The heavy order-total aggregations join wp_posts to wp_postmeta by repeated self-joins on meta_key. They are kept on Aurora MySQL and sent to a reader instead of being redesigned.
trade_offs.impact: The reports stay correct with no application change. They remain slower than the page-serving queries (911 ms per call for query `a0b655ea`), but at 0.03 calls per second they no longer compete with the writer.

trade_offs.description: The comment count of query `8c66eaee` moves from COUNT(*) over a post's comments to a counter item in PostCommentCounts, keyed by post and approval status. The comment insert (query `de9a7ba3`) writes the comment and adds 1 to the counter in one TransactWriteItems call.
trade_offs.impact: The count is one GetItem instead of a read of every matching comment, and it stays exact because the insert and the increment commit together. Every comment insert now writes 2 items in a transaction, billed at 2 write units per 1 KB per item. Changing a comment's approval status or deleting a comment must also adjust the counters; those writes belong to other queries and the application owns them. The counter table holds at most one item per post and status pair, at most 29651 items.

trade_offs.description: Comments and their meta rows share one item collection keyed by comment_id: the comment is the item with sort key COMMENT and each meta row is an item with sort key META# followed by the meta_id zero-padded to 20 digits. Query `65f7884e` reads a comment's meta rows in meta_id order from that partition; query `7346ea7e` reads the comment with GetItem.
trade_offs.impact: A comment and its meta rows live in one partition, so reading both costs one partition's capacity. The padding keeps the lexicographic sort key order equal to numeric meta_id order. An IN list of comment ids becomes one Query per id, run in parallel by the application. The source column comment_ID is an auto-increment; new comments need an application-generated numeric id.

trade_offs.description: Text columns stay inline in the items: comment_content is capped at 65535 bytes in the source and wp_comments averages 552 bytes per row against the 400 KB item limit; meta_value is a longtext whose table is estimated at 52429 bytes per row, also under the limit.
trade_offs.impact: No pointer attribute or S3 object is needed for these columns today. A comment_content value is at most 65535 bytes, so it always fits. A meta_value above 400 KB would fail to write, so the application stores such a value in S3 and keeps a pointer attribute.

trade_offs.description: API key authentication (query `1794daed`) reads through the ApiKeysByConsumerKey index, which projects user_id, permissions, consumer_secret and nonces so the read needs no base-table fetch. The last_access update (query `0452bed2`) changes no projected attribute, so it writes only the base item.
trade_offs.impact: The index lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a key created or changed by the application is visible to the authentication lookup after that delay, and the write path that must see the key at once reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem on key_id. The 248 writes per second of the last_access update run without row locks, replacing the source's lock waits of 46.68% of query time, and use about 50% of the 1,000 write units per second a partition accepts.

trade_offs.description: Query `329367a2` scanned wp_wc_tax_rate_classes. The 2 rows now sit in one partition under the constant key TAX_RATE_CLASS, with a sort key of name followed by the class id, so the read is one Query that returns them ordered by name.
trade_offs.impact: The scan is gone. All reads hit one partition value at 37.9 per second, about 0.6% of the 3,000 read units per second it accepts, which holds because the table has 2 rows. A new class must be written with the same constant partition key.

trade_offs.description: The two key-scoped writes, query `77cd1ad7` on wp_wc_reserved_stock and query `2264704d` on wp_woocommerce_downloadable_product_permissions, use order_id as the partition key of their tables. Each write Queries the order's items by key and then deletes or updates them item by item.
trade_offs.impact: These writes read only the items of one order, never the table. An order's partition holds all its stock reservations or permissions; the cardinality of order_id is unknown, so the figure for items per order comes from the data after migration. The set-based UPDATE becomes one UpdateItem per item with attribute_exists(permission_id), billed per item written; these writes run at 4.55 and 2.91 per second.

trade_offs.description: The log table wp_actionscheduler_logs is keyed by action_id with log_id as the sort key, and the insert (query `b05af520`) is a PutItem with attribute_not_exists(log_id). The source log_id is an auto-increment, so new entries need an application-generated, increasing id.
trade_offs.impact: Log entries of one action stay together and writes spread across actions, at 2.9 writes per second. No query in this group reads the logs back by action or by date, so the design adds no index for them; a time-based read would need a GSI on log_date_gmt.

trade_offs.description: wp_wc_product_meta_lookup becomes the table ProductMetaLookup keyed by product_id, and REPLACE INTO (query `d72966f8`) becomes a PutItem that overwrites the whole item. The secondary indexes of the source table (sku, price range, stock and sale flags) have no read query in this group, so none is created.
trade_offs.impact: Product filters by sku, price or stock status are not served by this design; they would need a GSI per filter or a search service. The 150 items average 618 bytes.

trade_offs.description: Posts and their metadata share one item collection in `wp_posts`: the post is the item with sort key `POST` and each metadata row is an item with sort key `META#<meta_key>`, both under the partition key `post_id`.
trade_offs.impact: Post lookups by ID (query `047e0146`) and metadata writes (query `126679dc`) address one partition key, and a later per-post read of the post with its metadata is one Query. A post update rewrites only the `POST` item, whose average source row is 711 B against the 400 KB item limit.

trade_offs.description: The key of each metadata table is (parent id, `meta_key`), so one item holds one value per key. The source allows several rows with the same post_id and meta_key, and the migration finds them before load.
trade_offs.impact: Keys with repeated rows are loaded as one item whose `meta_value` is a JSON list, and the application reads and writes those keys as lists. Updates by post and key (queries `ea7778db`, `2c0093ed`, `33dfdb12`, `4b856e29`, `3c5c8a79`) address one item through `UpdateItem`.

trade_offs.description: Increment and decrement updates on `meta_value` (queries `2c0093ed`, `33dfdb12`) run as `UpdateItem` with `ADD`, which needs a number. Keys updated this way are stored with the number type in `meta_value`; every other key stays a string.
trade_offs.impact: The application reads a counter key as a number. The update fails when the item does not exist (`attribute_exists(post_id)`), as the source `UPDATE` changes no row in that case.

trade_offs.description: Auto-increment IDs (`wp_posts.ID`, `wp_actionscheduler_actions.action_id`, the metadata `meta_id` columns) are assigned by the application as time-ordered 64-bit integers, and each insert (queries `445ec39b`, `7ead756f`) is a `PutItem` with `attribute_not_exists` on the key.
trade_offs.impact: New IDs are larger than every migrated ID and do not need a shared counter item, so inserts spread across partitions. The scheduled-action insert in the source also skips rows that a subquery finds; DynamoDB cannot run that subquery inside the write, so the application performs the duplicate-action lookup before calling `PutItem`. Lookups by hook and status are outside this design part.

trade_offs.description: Query `50b46567` read all metadata of a list of terms with full table scans in the source (7,741 scans). It becomes one Query per `term_id` on the `wp_termmeta` partition key, and the sort key is `meta_key` instead of `meta_id`.
trade_offs.impact: The application issues the per-term Queries in parallel and sorts the merged result by the retained `meta_id` attribute to keep the source order. Each Query reads the term's items only, so no Scan runs.

trade_offs.description: Large text columns stay inline: `post_content`, `post_content_filtered`, `post_excerpt`, `post_title`, `to_ping`, `pinged` and the `meta_value` columns. Average source rows are 711 B for posts, 144 B for post metadata and 131 B for order item metadata, against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: The migration checks each item's size before load and lists any item over 400 KB; the application stores the value of such an item in S3 and keeps the object key in the item. Reads of a post return the whole item, so a post read is billed on the full item size.

trade_offs.description: Query `3440484f` filters a post by ID and `post_type`. The key `post_id` identifies the item, so the read is a `GetItem` and the application compares `post_type` on the returned item.
trade_offs.impact: A post of another type returns an item the application discards, with no extra read, because the read is billed on the one item.

trade_offs.description: The usermeta IN-list read (query `3a74580e`) becomes one Query per user_id on wp_usermeta, keyed by user_id with umeta_id as the sort key.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB has no IN operator on a partition key, so the application issues one Query per user in the list and merges the results. Each Query returns that user's meta rows already ordered by umeta_id, which replaces the ORDER BY.

trade_offs.description: The meta_value column stays inline on wp_usermeta items: the table averages 16478 bytes per row against the 400 KB item limit, and the design counts it at 1 KB per item (1328 bytes per item).
trade_offs.impact: No S3 pointer is needed for the current data. A single meta value that grows past 400 KB fails the write, so the application checks the value size before it writes.

trade_offs.description: wp_woocommerce_order_items is keyed by order_item_id alone and carries no index on order_id, which the source table indexes. No query in this part reads order items by order_id.
trade_offs.impact: The application assigns order_item_id itself, because DynamoDB has no auto-increment column, and the PutItem fails with attribute_not_exists(order_item_id) if an id is reused. A read of all items of one order needs a GSI on order_id, added when such a query appears; until then it is not served.

trade_offs.description: The order_item_name column (text, 65535 bytes maximum) stays inline on wp_woocommerce_order_items: the table averages 129 bytes per row against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: Items stay far below the item limit, so no S3 pointer attribute is used. The design counts the column at 1 KB, giving 1291 bytes per item.

trade_offs.description: wp_term_relationships is keyed by object_id and term_taxonomy_id, and the source index on term_taxonomy_id alone is not carried over because query `0d20f1d9` reads by the full key.
trade_offs.impact: The link check is a single GetItem. Finding every object linked to one term is not served by this design; it needs a GSI on term_taxonomy_id, added when such a query appears.

trade_offs.description: `wp_options` becomes one DynamoDB table keyed by `option_name`, the column carrying the unique index in the source, so the lookups, upsert, update and delete (queries `66c96f95`, `e223aefb`, `ac34da34`, `a13f5749`, `216d92b3`) are single-item operations by key. The auto-increment `option_id` is kept as a plain attribute.
trade_offs.impact: Option names are unique by construction because DynamoDB enforces uniqueness on the primary key, so no sentinel items are needed. Nothing in the in-scope queries reads by `option_id`.

trade_offs.description: The autoload load (query `413c99e4`) reads the `OptionsByAutoload` index, partitioned on `autoload` and projecting `option_value`, so the Query returns about 247 items without a base-table fetch. `autoload` has few distinct values, so one partition value holds the loaded options; its read load of about 500 read units per second and write load of about 129 write units per second at design rates stay under the per-partition limits.
trade_offs.impact: The index lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a caller that needs the latest option reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem. Each upsert or update that changes `autoload` deletes and re-inserts the index entry, which doubles that write's index cost.

trade_offs.description: `option_value` (longtext) stays inline in the item. The table's average item is 360 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, and the schema-wide item size estimate is 1283 bytes with the text column counted at 1 KB.
trade_offs.impact: An option value larger than 400 KB cannot be stored in the item. The migration checks the largest `option_value` before load and moves any value near that limit to S3 with a pointer attribute.

trade_offs.description: The update by name (query `ac34da34`) carries `attribute_exists(option_name)`, matching the source UPDATE, which changes only a row that exists. The upsert (query `a13f5749`) is an unconditional PutItem that replaces the whole item.
trade_offs.impact: Every PutItem on an option carries all four attributes, because a Put replaces the item. An update for a missing option fails the condition instead of creating the item, and the caller falls back to the upsert path.

trade_offs.description: Posts, post metadata and options are cached with event-driven deletes plus a TTL of 10 to 60 minutes.
trade_offs.impact: After a settings or post change the cached entry stays until the write path deletes its key, and for at most the key's TTL if that delete fails. A read that must see the change before the delete reads Aurora MySQL, which serves every cache miss.

trade_offs.description: The term joins of queries `d5ae7abb`, `4481cc0c` and `2389b8a0` are precomputed per object and per term instead of joined at read time.
trade_offs.impact: Term data is stored in two shapes, a per-term hash and a per-object ID list. A term edit is visible in the per-object list after the application deletes it, and at the latest after the 10-minute TTL. Memory use grows with objects times taxonomy and ordering variants, about 24,000 small keys.

trade_offs.description: Scheduler action reads use TTLs of 15 and 30 seconds instead of delete-on-write, because the status of a row changes on every queue run.
trade_offs.impact: A cached action or queue list can show a status up to 30 seconds old. Claiming and status changes run only on Aurora MySQL, so a stale cache entry cannot cause an action to run twice.

trade_offs.description: Post list and title lookups (queries `f31a66f5`, `d4bf16d6` and `52da34b1`) are cached as sorted sets of IDs, one key per distinct status filter.
trade_offs.impact: Lists expire after 2 minutes, so a newly published post appears in a cached list up to 2 minutes later unless the read goes to Aurora MySQL. These queries return no rows on average, so most cached entries are empty results that save database calls but little data transfer.

trade_offs.description: Postmeta and order item meta are stored as one hash per parent with a JSON array of values per meta_key, not one key per row.
trade_offs.impact: One HGETALL replaces a 24 to 32 row index scan, and duplicate meta keys keep their meta_id order inside the array. A change to one meta row rewrites the whole hash on the next miss, so hashes with very many keys cost more to rebuild.

The secondary indexes of the source table (sku, price range, stock and sale flags) have no read query in this group, so none is created.
trade_offs.impact: Product filters by sku, price or stock status are not served by this design; they would need a GSI per filter or a search service. The 150 items average 618 bytes.

trade_offs.description: Posts and their metadata share one item collection in `wp_posts`: the post is the item with sort key `POST` and each metadata row is an item with sort key `META#<meta_key>`, both under the partition key `post_id`.
trade_offs.impact: Post lookups by ID (query `047e0146`) and metadata writes (query `126679dc`) address one partition key, and a later per-post read of the post with its metadata is one Query. A post update rewrites only the `POST` item, whose average source row is 711 B against the 400 KB item limit.

trade_offs.description: The key of each metadata table is (parent id, `meta_key`), so one item holds one value per key. The source allows several rows with the same post_id and meta_key, and the migration finds them before load.
trade_offs.impact: Keys with repeated rows are loaded as one item whose `meta_value` is a JSON list, and the application reads and writes those keys as lists. Updates by post and key (queries `ea7778db`, `2c0093ed`, `33dfdb12`, `4b856e29`, `3c5c8a79`) address one item through `UpdateItem`.

trade_offs.description: Increment and decrement updates on `meta_value` (queries `2c0093ed`, `33dfdb12`) run as `UpdateItem` with `ADD`, which needs a number. Keys updated this way are stored with the number type in `meta_value`; every other key stays a string.
trade_offs.impact: The application reads a counter key as a number. The update fails when the item does not exist (`attribute_exists(post_id)`), as the source `UPDATE` changes no row in that case.

trade_offs.description: Auto-increment IDs (`wp_posts.ID`, `wp_actionscheduler_actions.action_id`, the metadata `meta_id` columns) are assigned by the application as time-ordered 64-bit integers, and each insert (queries `445ec39b`, `7ead756f`) is a `PutItem` with `attribute_not_exists` on the key.
trade_offs.impact: New IDs are larger than every migrated ID and do not need a shared counter item, so inserts spread across partitions. The scheduled-action insert in the source also skips rows that a subquery finds; DynamoDB cannot run that subquery inside the write, so the application performs the duplicate-action lookup before calling `PutItem`. Lookups by hook and status are outside this design part.

trade_offs.description: Query `50b46567` read all metadata of a list of terms with full table scans in the source (7,741 scans). It becomes one Query per `term_id` on the `wp_termmeta` partition key, and the sort key is `meta_key` instead of `meta_id`.
trade_offs.impact: The application issues the per-term Queries in parallel and sorts the merged result by the retained `meta_id` attribute to keep the source order. Each Query reads the term's items only, so no Scan runs.

trade_offs.description: Large text columns stay inline: `post_content`, `post_content_filtered`, `post_excerpt`, `post_title`, `to_ping`, `pinged` and the `meta_value` columns. Average source rows are 711 B for posts, 144 B for post metadata and 131 B for order item metadata, against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: The migration checks each item's size before load and lists any item over 400 KB; the application stores the value of such an item in S3 and keeps the object key in the item. Reads of a post return the whole item, so a post read is billed on the full item size.

trade_offs.description: Query `3440484f` filters a post by ID and `post_type`. The key `post_id` identifies the item, so the read is a `GetItem` and the application compares `post_type` on the returned item.
trade_offs.impact: A post of another type returns an item the application discards, with no extra read, because the read is billed on the one item.

trade_offs.description: The usermeta IN-list read (query `3a74580e`) becomes one Query per user_id on wp_usermeta, keyed by user_id with umeta_id as the sort key.
trade_offs.impact: DynamoDB has no IN operator on a partition key, so the application issues one Query per user in the list and merges the results. Each Query returns that user's meta rows already ordered by umeta_id, which replaces the ORDER BY.

trade_offs.description: The meta_value column stays inline on wp_usermeta items: the table averages 16478 bytes per row against the 400 KB item limit, and the design counts it at 1 KB per item (1328 bytes per item).
trade_offs.impact: No S3 pointer is needed for the current data. A single meta value that grows past 400 KB fails the write, so the application checks the value size before it writes.

trade_offs.description: wp_woocommerce_order_items is keyed by order_item_id alone and carries no index on order_id, which the source table indexes. No query in this part reads order items by order_id.
trade_offs.impact: The application assigns order_item_id itself, because DynamoDB has no auto-increment column, and the PutItem fails with attribute_not_exists(order_item_id) if an id is reused. A read of all items of one order needs a GSI on order_id, added when such a query appears; until then it is not served.

trade_offs.description: The order_item_name column (text, 65535 bytes maximum) stays inline on wp_woocommerce_order_items: the table averages 129 bytes per row against the 400 KB item limit.
trade_offs.impact: Items stay far below the item limit, so no S3 pointer attribute is used. The design counts the column at 1 KB, giving 1291 bytes per item.

trade_offs.description: wp_term_relationships is keyed by object_id and term_taxonomy_id, and the source index on term_taxonomy_id alone is not carried over because query `0d20f1d9` reads by the full key.
trade_offs.impact: The link check is a single GetItem. Finding every object linked to one term is not served by this design; it needs a GSI on term_taxonomy_id, added when such a query appears.

trade_offs.description: `wp_options` becomes one DynamoDB table keyed by `option_name`, the column carrying the unique index in the source, so the lookups, upsert, update and delete (queries `66c96f95`, `e223aefb`, `ac34da34`, `a13f5749`, `216d92b3`) are single-item operations by key. The auto-increment `option_id` is kept as a plain attribute.
trade_offs.impact: Option names are unique by construction because DynamoDB enforces uniqueness on the primary key, so no sentinel items are needed. Nothing in the in-scope queries reads by `option_id`.

trade_offs.description: The autoload load (query `413c99e4`) reads the `OptionsByAutoload` index, partitioned on `autoload` and projecting `option_value`, so the Query returns about 247 items without a base-table fetch. `autoload` has few distinct values, so one partition value holds the loaded options; its read load of about 500 read units per second and write load of about 129 write units per second at design rates stay under the per-partition limits.
trade_offs.impact: The index lags the base table until DynamoDB applies each write to it; a caller that needs the latest option reads the base item with a strongly consistent GetItem. Each upsert or update that changes `autoload` deletes and re-inserts the index entry, which doubles that write's index cost.

trade_offs.description: `option_value` (longtext) stays inline in the item. The table's average item is 360 bytes against the 400 KB item limit, and the schema-wide item size estimate is 1283 bytes with the text column counted at 1 KB.
trade_offs.impact: An option value larger than 400 KB cannot be stored in the item. The migration checks the largest `option_value` before load and moves any value near that limit to S3 with a pointer attribute.

trade_offs.description: The update by name (query `ac34da34`) carries `attribute_exists(option_name)`, matching the source UPDATE, which changes only a row that exists. The upsert (query `a13f5749`) is an unconditional PutItem that replaces the whole item.
trade_offs.impact: Every PutItem on an option carries all four attributes, because a Put replaces the item. An update for a missing option fails the condition instead of creating the item, and the caller falls back to the upsert path.

trade_offs.description: Posts, post metadata and options are cached with event-driven deletes plus a TTL of 10 to 60 minutes.
trade_offs.impact: After a settings or post change the cached entry stays until the write path deletes its key, and for at most the key's TTL if that delete fails. A read that must see the change before the delete reads Aurora MySQL, which serves every cache miss.

trade_offs.description: The term joins of queries `d5ae7abb`, `4481cc0c` and `2389b8a0` are precomputed per object and per term instead of joined at read time.
trade_offs.impact: Term data is stored in two shapes, a per-term hash and a per-object ID list. A term edit is visible in the per-object list after the application deletes it, and at the latest after the 10-minute TTL. Memory use grows with objects times taxonomy and ordering variants, about 24,000 small keys.

trade_offs.description: Scheduler action reads use TTLs of 15 and 30 seconds instead of delete-on-write, because the status of a row changes on every queue run.
trade_offs.impact: A cached action or queue list can show a status up to 30 seconds old. Claiming and status changes run only on Aurora MySQL, so a stale cache entry cannot cause an action to run twice.

trade_offs.description: Post list and title lookups (queries `f31a66f5`, `d4bf16d6` and `52da34b1`) are cached as sorted sets of IDs, one key per distinct status filter.
trade_offs.impact: Lists expire after 2 minutes, so a newly published post appears in a cached list up to 2 minutes later unless the read goes to Aurora MySQL. These queries return no rows on average, so most cached entries are empty results that save database calls but little data transfer.

trade_offs.description: Postmeta and order item meta are stored as one hash per parent with a JSON array of values per meta_key, not one key per row.
trade_offs.impact: One HGETALL replaces a 24 to 32 row index scan, and duplicate meta keys keep their meta_id order inside the array. A change to one meta row rewrites the whole hash on the next miss, so hashes with very many keys cost more to rebuild.

migration_waves.rationale: The whole source database (MySQL 8.0.45) moves 1:1 to Aurora MySQL: same engine family. The collector reports engine and version only; feature compatibility is not assessed here. 67 queries (62.6%) remain on Aurora MySQL once later waves have moved their share; later waves move subsets of these 50 tables and views out of Aurora MySQL. 22 of these tables and views are mapped to a target engine in the migration map; later waves move 15 of the 50 off Aurora MySQL, and the other 35 stay on Aurora MySQL.

migration_waves.title: Cache hot reads with ElastiCache
migration_waves.rationale: 20 hot reads (83.4% of calls), cache-aside in front of Aurora MySQL in wave 2, then DynamoDB once wave 3 moves these reads: no data migration, fully reversible. It takes the read pressure off before the data migrations that follow. These reads belong to queries that move in wave 1 (Aurora MySQL) and wave 3 (DynamoDB); this share overlaps the owner shares, which alone sum to 100%.
